title: Pauline’s super easy pitch to households
full_text:
Australians would be able to claw back thousands of dollars a year under a One Nation policy to immediately divert a portion of super payments back to workers.
Pauline Hanson’s party wants renters and mortgage holders to be allowed to divert a quarter of their future compulsory super contributions into take-home pay.
The proposed exception would run for three years.
For a couple earning a combined $168,000, the scheme would deliver about $4300 a year after tax, or $82 a week. An individual worker earning $90,500 would pocket about $2300 extra, or $44 a week.
The policy sets up a new battlefront on superannuation, with early access super schemes attacked in the past for their potential to fuel inflation and diminish retirement savings.
The controversial pitch is aimed directly at households being squeezed by higher housing costs, power bills and other living expenses.
Ms Hanson said Australians needed relief now.
“People are working their guts out and they’re still struggling. They need help today,” she said. “We face interest rates going up, warnings everywhere that rents are going to keep rising, insurance up … everything is getting more expensive and everyone knows it, but who is doing anything about it?
“Well, we want to. It shouldn’t just be about handouts – just stop taking money off people when they need it to survive. Inflation is hurting and Labor’s incompetence is making life harder.
“One Nation wants to give people some breathing room.” Existing super balances would be quarantined from the scheme. Employers would keep paying the full 12 per cent compulsory contribution, but workers who took up the option would have the equivalent of up to three percentage points redirected by their super fund into their bank account. That would leave at least 9 per cent invested for retirement.
The proposal has a major tax break, which One Nation said would have no impact on the budget. Instead of the redirected money being taxed as normal wages, it would retain the concessional super tax treatment, typically 15 per cent.
One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce said the retirement system had lost sight of the financial emergency confronting families.
“There’s no point telling a family they’ll be better off in retirement if they can’t afford the mortgage or their rent payment today,” he said. “A good retirement starts with keeping a roof over your head.” Mr Joyce said the measure would be limited to Australians paying rent or a mortgage on the home in which they lived, with investment properties excluded.
Partners who contributed to household housing costs would qualify, even if their name was not formally listed on the lease or mortgage.
Workers would deal directly with their super fund, which would verify their housing costs, calculate the payment and deposit the money into their bank account.
The entitlement would be capped at 36 months in total and could not be reset by changing jobs or super funds. EDITORIAL PAGE 34
